title: TypeScript SDK: pragmatic bridge for AsyncIterator <-> Web Streams with resumable framing
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Purpose: provide a pragmatic, low-footprint adapter and guidance that makes it straightforward for Redwood TypeScript SDK consumers to convert between AsyncIterator-based consumers (common in Node/older libs) and the Web Streams API (common in browsers and modern runtimes). The adapter must preserve cancellation semantics, resume from last checkpointed chunk when safe, and expose explicit framing so implementers can do incremental parsing or stable checkpointing. This ticket covers design, reference implementation, tests, examples, and rollout steps.
acceptance_criteria: Provide a minimal adapter API that maps AsyncIterator<T> to ReadableStream<T> and vice versa with clear cancellation propagation.
Implement a compact framing protocol (length-prefixed or boundary tokens) and provide utilities for common framing strategies (newline-delimited JSON, length-prefixed, chunk-marker).
Resume protocol: support a resume handshake where consumer can request last-ack token to resume a partially-processed stream without duplication or token loss for idempotent flows.
Documentation: include three examples (Node-only AsyncIterator consumer, Browser ReadableStream consumer, and a hybrid server that demultiplexes both).
Integration tests that simulate intermittent network failures and validate resume correctness and no double-delivery for idempotent payloads.
Performance regression tests to ensure the adapter adds <8% median latency at 1–256 concurrent streams on our CI harness compared to baseline passthrough.
Code reviewed, merged, and feature-flag gated behind experimental streaming compatibility in the 2026.03 SDK release.
design_decisions: Keep runtime surface minimal: two adapters `asyncIterToWebStream` and `webStreamToAsyncIter` + framing helpers. No heavy runtime state machines.
Framing: default to newline-delimited JSON for ergonomics, provide `LengthPrefixed` utility for binary + efficiency-sensitive flows.
Resumption token: allow producers to emit opaque checkpoint tokens (string) interleaved with payloads; consumers can request resume with last token.
Cancellation: map AbortSignal to AsyncIterator return() and ReadableStream controller.close(); ensure upstream errors propagate to both sides.

Backpressure semantics: when converting AsyncIterator -> ReadableStream, use controller.enqueue and await `iter.next()` only when desired size indicates capacity; use internal buffer size param (default 1).
Security: leave encryption/validation of resume tokens to application layer; SDK will only carry opaque tokens and verify presence/format where applicable.
Trade-offs: keeping adapter small avoids coupling to runtime schedulers but requires consumers to wire advanced batching themselves; acceptable for experimental roll-out.
compatibility_matrix: Bun - partial; requires ReadableStream polyfill for some older Bun versions
Browser (Chrome/Firefox/Safari latest) - supported for ReadableStream consumers
Older Node runtimes without Web Streams - supported via small polyfill included in examples (explicit opt-in).
implementation_notes:
Core API shape (TS):

export function asyncIterToWebStream<T>(source: AsyncIterable<T>, options?: { highWaterMark?: number, frame?: FrameStrategy<T>, onCheckpoint?: (token: string) => void }): ReadableStream<T>

export function webStreamToAsyncIter<T>(stream: ReadableStream<T>, options?: { signal?: AbortSignal, frame?: FrameStrategy<T> }): AsyncIterable<T>

Framing helpers: `newlineJsonFrame()`, `lengthPrefixedFrame()` implemented as composable transform utilities. Each returns an object with `encode(payload): Uint8Array|string` and `decode(buffer): {items: T[], remainder: Uint8Array|string}` so callers can maintain partial buffers.

Resume handshake: lightweight protocol where producers can emit special control records `{__checkpoint__: '<token>'}` (configurable key) between payloads; consumer stores last token after successful processing and can supply `?resume_token=<token>` on subsequent connections. SDK will provide `serializeCheckpoint`/`parseCheckpoint` helpers but not enforce transport-layer semantics.

Performance: avoid per-chunk micro-allocations where possible. Use a pooled buffer path in `lengthPrefixedFrame` for binary workloads. Add a small benchmark harness under `sdk/bench/stream-interop` that runs in CI.
Docs: write a single-page guide in the SDK docs site with diagrams showing the mapping of signals, return()/cancel paths, and resume token lifecycle.
testing_plan: Unit tests for framing helpers: edge cases (partial frames, multi-frame buffer, empty frames).

Integration tests: orchestrate a producer that emits 10k small JSON messages; kill connection mid-stream; restart with resume token and assert consumer receives remaining messages exactly once for idempotent flow.
Chaos tests: CI scenario that injects network latency and random connection drops at 1s–5s intervals across 100 concurrent streams.
Fuzz tests for malformed resume tokens and unexpected control records. SDK should surface clear errors (400-ish) but not crash the host process.
Benchmark: measure p95 token latency and CPU overhead at multiple concurrency points and compare to baseline (direct ReadableStream usage).
rollout_plan: Merge behind feature flag `experimental.streamInterop` default off.
Publish canary npm with tag `experimental-streaming` for internal teams and early partners.
Collect telemetry for adapter usage, average buffer sizes, resume success/failure rates (opt-in in telemetry).
After 2 weeks of internal usage and no critical regressions, flip flag on for general availability in sdk-2026.03.
Follow-up: gather feedback and iterate on ergonomics (likely to add `createStreamConsumer` helper for common patterns).
